newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union has second crack at jobs alliance.
newsitem.headline: German union has second crack at jobs alliance.

text.p: A moderate 1997 wage demand lodged by IG Metall is being seen as an attempt by Germany's largest union to re-launch Germany's failed "Alliance for Jobs" plan -- but this time without the rhetoric or the politicians.

Economists said on Wednesday the metal and engineering union's offer to accept a real wage freeze in return for measures to boost job security echoed the goals of the grand scheme that foundered in May -- but looked more pragmatic.
"The methods this time seem more appropriate to an economy which after all is not centrally planned," said Thomas Mayer, senior economist at the Frankfurt office of Goldman Sachs.
The earlier initiative, which gained government backing, ran across industry sectors in its aim of slashing unemployment while curbing wage rises and public spending.

But the alliance, which never really got the full support of employers, eventually collapsed earlier this year when it became clear that the government was determined to slash budget deficits regardless of what the unions wanted.

IG Metall chairman Klaus Zwickel on Tuesday acknowledged that the union's 1997 wage bargaining position was "consistent" with the aims of the "Alliance for Jobs" in its trade-off between job protection and wage rises.

But with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's austerity package now passed by parliament, IG Metall has had little option but to return to a sector-specific strategy aimed at securing a deal for 3.5 million workers in the metal and engineering sectors.

"Before, Zwickel was hoping to sit down at a round table with government and employers and work out an overall formula. But he should know it can't work like that in this country," Goldman Sachs' Mayer said.

The current row over sick pay allowances, where engineering firms have decided not to implement a new law cutting sick payments but chemical giant BASF AG has, only emphasises the difficulty of imposing deals across sectors.

IG Metall's new proposal that up to three percentage points of its overall 4.5-5.0 percent wage claim be used for job security measures implies that it could accept a 1997 wage increase barely higher than inflation.

That is something the Gesamtmetall employers' federation has said it would be prepared to discuss. The sticking point is that whereas IG Metall wants money spent on job protection measures, Gesamtmetall wants contractual labour costs to fall.
Despite IG Metall's victory earlier this week in forcing Gesamtmetall to climb down on sick pay for now, analysts argue that the call for cuts in labour costs will simply not go away.
"One way or another there will have to be a squeeze on wage costs," Midlands Global Research international economist Ros Lifton said.
